description: The Wolfram Language distinguishes exact numbers (integers, rationals, algebraic and symbolic constants) from approximate machine and arbitrary-precision reals, and tracks precision automatically through a computation. This category covers numeric evaluation and precision control, rounding and integer division, complex number parts, digit and base representations, and the aggregation functions Total, Accumulate and Differences.

tools.name: N
tools.description: Converts an exact or symbolic expression to an approximate number. N[expr] uses machine precision (about 16 digits), while N[expr, n] performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic carrying roughly n significant digits and tracking error through the computation. It is the bridge from symbolic to numeric work and is applied automatically by plotting and numeric solvers.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Requested number of significant digits of precision; omit for machine precision.

tools.notes: N[expr, n] with n greater than $MachinePrecision switches to software arbitrary-precision arithmetic, which is slower but tracks precision loss. If the result loses too many digits, raise $MaxExtraPrecision.

tools.name: Rationalize
tools.description: Converts an approximate real number to a nearby rational. Rationalize[x] returns a rational only if one is very close to x, otherwise it returns x unchanged; Rationalize[x, dx] finds the simplest rational within tolerance dx. Rationalize[x, 0] always produces the exact rational corresponding to the binary floating-point value or the simplest one agreeing to the given precision.
tools.notes: Rationalizing before symbolic work often turns an unsolvable numeric problem into an exact one; combine with Together and Simplify.

tools.name: Round
tools.description: Rounds a number to the nearest integer, or to the nearest multiple of a given increment. Round uses banker's rounding: exact halves go to the nearest even integer, so Round[0.5] is 0 and Round[1.5] is 2. It is Listable and works on exact, machine and arbitrary-precision numbers.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Increment to round to, e.g. 0.01 for two decimal places or 5 for multiples of five.

tools.notes: The even-rounding rule surprises people expecting Round[0.5] == 1; use Floor[x + 1/2] for half-up rounding.

tools.name: Floor
tools.description: Gives the greatest integer less than or equal to a number, so it always rounds toward negative infinity. Floor[x, a] gives the greatest multiple of a that does not exceed x, which is the general way to quantize downward. It is Listable and exact for rational and symbolic input.
tools.notes: Floor differs from IntegerPart for negative numbers: Floor[-2.7] is -3 while IntegerPart[-2.7] is -2.

tools.name: Ceiling
tools.description: Gives the smallest integer greater than or equal to a number, rounding toward positive infinity. Ceiling[x, a] rounds up to the next multiple of a. It is the standard way to compute how many fixed-size blocks are needed to cover a quantity.

tools.name: IntegerPart
tools.description: Gives the integer part of a number obtained by truncating toward zero, so IntegerPart[-2.7] is -2. Together with FractionalPart it decomposes any real as x == IntegerPart[x] + FractionalPart[x]. For complex numbers it acts on real and imaginary parts separately.
tools.notes: Use Floor when you need rounding toward negative infinity, and Quotient for integer division with a specified sign convention.

tools.name: FractionalPart
tools.description: Gives the fractional part of a number, with the same sign as the number itself, so FractionalPart[-2.7] is -0.7. It is the complement of IntegerPart. Use Mod[x, 1] instead when you want a result that is always non-negative.

tools.name: Abs
tools.description: Gives the absolute value of a real number or the modulus of a complex number. It stays symbolic for symbolic arguments unless assumptions are supplied, so Abs[x] does not simplify to x without knowing x is real and non-negative. Abs is Listable and works on Quantity objects.
tools.example:
Abs[-3]
Abs[3 + 4 I]
Abs[-2.5]
Simplify[Abs[x], x > 0]
Abs[{-1, 2, -3}]
tools.notes: For symbolic simplification use Assuming[x \[Element] Reals, ...] or RealAbs, which assumes a real argument and is differentiable in the real sense.

tools.name: Sign
tools.description: Gives -1, 0 or 1 according to the sign of a real number, and z/Abs[z] for a nonzero complex number. It remains symbolic for symbolic input unless assumptions determine the sign. Sign is Listable and commonly used to extract direction from a numeric result.
tools.example:
Sign[-3.2]
Sign[0]
Sign[3 + 4 I]
Simplify[Sign[x], x < 0]
Sign /@ Differences[{1, 3, 2}]

tools.name: Mod
tools.description: Gives the remainder of m divided by n, with the result always having the same sign as n, so Mod[-7, 3] is 2. A third argument shifts the output range, so Mod[x, n, 1] gives results from 1 to n. Mod works for integers, rationals, reals and Gaussian integers and is Listable.

parameters.name: d
parameters.description: Lower bound of the output interval; the result lies in [d, d + n).

tools.notes: Mod's sign convention differs from C's % operator. PowerMod computes modular powers efficiently for large exponents.

tools.name: Quotient
tools.description: Gives the integer quotient of m divided by n, consistent with Mod so that n Quotient[m, n] + Mod[m, n] == m always holds. A third argument offsets the range in the same way as Mod's third argument. Rounding is toward negative infinity for positive n.

tools.name: QuotientRemainder
tools.description: Returns the pair {Quotient[m, n], Mod[m, n]} in a single call, which is faster than computing both separately and keeps them consistent. It is the natural primitive for converting a total into units and remainder, such as seconds into minutes and seconds. Like Mod and Quotient it is Listable.

tools.name: Divisible
tools.description: Tests whether one number divides another exactly, returning True or False. It works for integers, rationals, Gaussian integers and polynomials, and is Listable so it tests whole lists at once. It is clearer than writing Mod[n, d] == 0.
tools.example:
Divisible[12, 4]
Divisible[13, 4]
Select[Range[30], Divisible[#, 7] &]
Divisible[x^2 - 1, x - 1]

tools.name: GCD
tools.description: Gives the greatest common divisor of any number of integers, rationals or Gaussian integers, computed with a fast Euclidean algorithm. GCD of a list requires Apply, as in GCD @@ list. PolynomialGCD is the corresponding operation for polynomials.
tools.notes: ExtendedGCD additionally returns the Bezout coefficients, which is what you need for modular inverses and Diophantine equations.

tools.name: LCM
tools.description: Gives the least common multiple of any number of integers or rationals. Like GCD it must be applied to a list with @@ when the arguments arrive as a list. It is used for combining periods, finding common denominators and synchronizing cycles.

tools.name: Max
tools.description: Gives the largest of the supplied values, flattening any lists it is given, so Max[{1, 5}, 3] works directly without Apply. With symbolic arguments it stays unevaluated or partially simplifies. Max[] returns -Infinity, which makes it a safe identity for folds.
tools.notes: Unlike most list functions Max flattens its arguments, so Max[{{1,2},{3,4}}] gives 4 rather than a row-wise result; use Map for per-row maxima.

tools.name: Min
tools.description: Gives the smallest of the supplied values, flattening lists in the same way as Max. Min[] returns Infinity. Together with Max it is used for clamping, range computations and simple optimization over discrete sets.
tools.notes: MinMax[list] returns {min, max} in one pass, which is faster than calling both functions.

tools.name: Total
tools.description: Adds up the elements of a list. Total[list] sums the top level, Total[list, n] sums down to level n, Total[list, {n}] sums only level n, and Total[m, {1}] or Total[m, {2}] gives column or row sums of a matrix. It is much faster than Plus @@ for packed numeric arrays.
tools.usage:
Total[list]
Total[list, n]
Total[list, {n}]
Total[list, Infinity]
tools.notes: Total of a matrix without a level gives the vector of column sums, which is Total[m, {1}]; use Total[m, {2}] for row sums.

tools.name: Accumulate
tools.description: Gives the list of cumulative sums, so Accumulate[{a, b, c}] is {a, a+b, a+b+c}. It is a fast built-in equivalent of Rest[FoldList[Plus, 0, list]] and works on packed numeric arrays and matrices. Use it for running totals, cumulative distributions and prefix sums.
tools.notes: FoldList[f, x, list] generalizes Accumulate to any binary operation, e.g. FoldList[Times, list] for a running product.

tools.name: Differences
tools.description: Gives the successive differences of a list, returning a list one element shorter. Differences[list, n] applies the operation n times to give n-th order differences, and a step specification supports lagged differences. It is the discrete derivative and the inverse of Accumulate.
tools.usage:
Differences[list]
Differences[list, n]
Differences[list, n, s]
tools.notes: Ratios is the multiplicative analogue. For a time series with time stamps, use the TimeSeries framework or Differences on the values only.

tools.name: Clip
tools.description: Limits a value to a range, returning -1 or 1 outside {-1, 1} by default or the supplied bounds. Clip[x, {min, max}] clamps to that interval and Clip[x, {min, max}, {vmin, vmax}] substitutes different values outside it. It is Listable, so it clamps whole arrays elementwise.
tools.usage:
Clip[x]
Clip[x, {min, max}]
Clip[x, {min, max}, {vmin, vmax}]

tools.name: Chop
tools.description: Replaces approximate real numbers smaller than a tolerance (10^-10 by default) by exact zero. It is the standard cleanup for numerical results where round-off leaves tiny nonzero residue, especially the imaginary parts of results that should be real. A second argument sets the tolerance.
tools.example:
Chop[1.0 + 1.*^-15 I]
Chop[N[Sin[Pi]]]
Chop[Eigenvalues[m], 10^-8]
Chop[Inverse[m] . m - IdentityMatrix[3]]
tools.notes: Chop only affects approximate numbers, never exact ones, and it can hide genuinely small results, so choose the tolerance deliberately.

tools.name: Re
tools.description: Gives the real part of a complex number. For symbolic arguments it stays unevaluated unless assumptions or ComplexExpand determine the structure. Re is Listable and threads over arrays automatically.
tools.example:
Re[3 + 4 I]
Re[Exp[I Pi/3]] // N
ComplexExpand[Re[(a + I b)^2]]
Re[Eigenvalues[m]]
tools.notes: Use ComplexExpand or Assuming[Element[x, Reals], ...] to get Re and Im to simplify symbolic expressions.

tools.name: Im
tools.description: Gives the imaginary part of a complex number, as a real number without the I factor. Like Re it remains symbolic without assumptions. Together with Re it decomposes any complex value, and with Abs and Arg it gives the polar description.
tools.example:
Im[3 + 4 I]
Im[Exp[I x]] // ComplexExpand
Chop[Im[roots]]
Im[{1 + I, 2 - 3 I}]

tools.name: Conjugate
tools.description: Gives the complex conjugate, negating the imaginary part. For symbolic expressions it stays unevaluated unless the variables are known to be real. It is the elementwise operation underlying ConjugateTranspose for matrices.
tools.example:
Conjugate[3 + 4 I]
Conjugate[Exp[I x]]
Simplify[Conjugate[x + I y], {x, y} \[Element] Reals]
Conjugate[{1 + I, 2 I}]
tools.notes: z Conjugate[z] equals Abs[z]^2; use ComplexExpand to force simplification with real symbols.

tools.name: Arg
tools.description: Gives the argument (phase angle) of a complex number in radians, in the range -Pi to Pi. Arg[0] is 0. Together with Abs it provides the polar form, and AbsArg returns both at once.
tools.example:
Arg[1 + I]
Arg[-1]
Arg[Exp[2 I]]
AbsArg[3 + 4 I]
Arg[{I, -I}]
tools.notes: The branch cut is along the negative real axis, so Arg jumps by 2 Pi there; use Unwrap on a list of phases from a continuous signal.

tools.name: Precision
tools.description: Gives the number of significant decimal digits known to be correct in an approximate number. Machine-precision numbers return the symbol MachinePrecision, exact numbers return Infinity, and arbitrary-precision numbers return a real number that decreases as precision is lost. It is the primary diagnostic when a numerical computation degrades.
tools.example:
Precision[1.5]
Precision[N[Pi, 50]]
Precision[1/3]
Precision[N[Pi, 50] - N[Pi, 50]]
Precision /@ {1.0, 1, N[Pi, 30]}
tools.notes: Precision is relative (significant digits) while Accuracy is absolute (digits after the decimal point); both matter near zero.

tools.name: Accuracy
tools.description: Gives the number of correct digits to the right of the decimal point in an approximate number, i.e. absolute rather than relative error. Exact numbers have infinite accuracy and the value 0.0 has finite accuracy but zero precision. Use it when the size of the absolute error is what matters.

tools.name: SetPrecision
tools.description: Returns a number with its precision reset to the requested number of digits, padding with the actual binary digits of the stored value when raising precision. Raising precision does not create new correct digits, so it must be used carefully; the reliable path is to recompute from exact input with N[expr, n]. SetAccuracy is the absolute-error counterpart.
tools.notes: SetPrecision[0.1, 40] exposes the binary representation error of 0.1 rather than giving 40 correct digits of one tenth.

tools.name: MachinePrecision
tools.description: A symbol representing the precision of machine double-precision numbers, returned by Precision for ordinary reals such as 1.5. Passing it to N, as N[expr, MachinePrecision], forces machine arithmetic. MachineNumberQ tests whether a value is stored in machine format.

tools.name: $MachinePrecision
tools.description: A global constant giving the number of decimal digits of precision in a machine number on the current system, normally about 15.9546. Related system constants are $MachineEpsilon, $MaxMachineNumber and $MinMachineNumber. Use it to decide whether a requested precision will use hardware or software arithmetic.
tools.notes: $MaxExtraPrecision (default 50) limits how many extra digits arbitrary-precision evaluation may use internally; raise it in a Block when N fails to converge.

tools.name: RealDigits
tools.description: Gives the digits of a real number as {digitlist, exponent}, where the exponent locates the decimal point. A base argument produces digits in any base, and a length argument limits how many digits are computed. Repeating decimals are returned with the repeating block wrapped in a list.
tools.usage:
RealDigits[x]
RealDigits[x, b]
RealDigits[x, b, len]
RealDigits[x, b, len, n]
tools.notes: FromDigits inverts RealDigits. For integers use IntegerDigits, which has a simpler return format.

tools.name: IntegerDigits
tools.description: Gives the list of digits of an integer in a specified base, most significant first. A length argument pads with leading zeros to a fixed width, which is useful for binary and hexadecimal formatting. It is Listable over the number argument.
tools.usage:
IntegerDigits[n]
IntegerDigits[n, b]
IntegerDigits[n, b, len]
tools.notes: IntegerString[n, b] gives the same information as a string, with letters for digits above 9.

tools.name: FromDigits
tools.description: Reconstructs a number from a list of digits in a given base, and also parses a string of digits into an integer. FromDigits[{digits, exp}, b] inverts the output of RealDigits. It is the standard way to convert between digit representations and numbers.
tools.usage:
FromDigits[list]
FromDigits[list, b]
FromDigits["string"]
FromDigits["string", b]

tools.name: BaseForm
tools.description: Displays a number in a specified base, showing the base as a subscript. It is a formatting wrapper only: the result prints in the chosen base but is not itself a number for further computation. Use IntegerString or IntegerDigits when you need the representation as data.
tools.notes: Base-n literals can also be written directly as 2^^1010 or 16^^ff, which are ordinary numbers rather than formatting wrappers.

tools.name: NumberForm
tools.description: Formats a number for display with a given number of significant digits and detailed control over separators, signs, padding and exponent style. NumberForm[x, {n, f}] shows n total digits with f after the decimal point, which is how fixed-decimal tables are produced. The result is a formatting object, so convert with ToString when a plain string is needed.
tools.usage:
NumberForm[x, n]
NumberForm[x, {n, f}]
NumberForm[x, opts]

parameters.name: DigitBlock
parameters.description: Group digits into blocks of this size, e.g. 3 for thousands separators.

parameters.name: NumberSigns
parameters.description: Strings to use for negative and positive numbers.

parameters.name: ExponentFunction
parameters.description: Function controlling when scientific notation is used; use (Null &) to suppress it.

tools.example:
NumberForm[N[Pi], 3]
NumberForm[1234.5678, {6, 2}]
NumberForm[1234567, DigitBlock -> 3, NumberSeparator -> ","]
ToString[NumberForm[3.14159, 3]]
tools.notes: Related formatting wrappers include ScientificForm, EngineeringForm, AccountingForm, PercentForm and PaddedForm.

tools.name: ScientificForm
tools.description: Displays a number in scientific notation with a single digit before the decimal point and an explicit power of ten. An optional digit count limits the mantissa precision, and the same options as NumberForm apply. EngineeringForm is the variant that uses exponents that are multiples of three.

tools.name: NumericQ
tools.description: Tests whether an expression can be evaluated to a number by N, returning True for Pi, Sqrt[2] and E as well as for explicit numbers. It is broader than NumberQ, which is True only for expressions that are already numeric objects. Use NumericQ in patterns for functions that will call N internally.
tools.example:
NumericQ[Pi]
NumberQ[Pi]
NumericQ[Sqrt[2] + Log[3]]
f[x_?NumericQ] := NIntegrate[Sin[t], {t, 0, x}];
NumericQ[x]
tools.notes: Defining a numeric function with the _?NumericQ pattern is the standard way to stop NIntegrate, FindRoot and Plot from trying to evaluate it symbolically.
